query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled subsolvus annealing treatment of an equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy will induce nanoscale chemical ordering (or coherent precipitate formation) that creates effective domain wall pinning centers and, consequently, increases the coercivity relative to the as-cast baseline alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy with high saturation magnetization but low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Apply a subsolvus annealing treatment at temperatures between 500 and 700 °C for a time period optimized to trigger nanoscale ordering without causing phase coarsening.
generation.conditions: The alloy is annealed under a thermally stable regime at 500–700 °C, below the coarsening threshold, and then cooled under controlled conditions. Room temperature magnetic characterization is performed after the treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale chemical ordering and/or formation of finely dispersed coherent precipitates that act as domain wall pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment promotes local atomic rearrangement within the alloy, inducing lattice distortions and forming ordered nano-domains or coherent precipitates. These microstructural features hinder domain wall motion, thereby enhancing magnetocrystalline anisotropy and elevating the coercive field.
generation.predicted_outcome: The annealed alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly increased coercivity compared to the as-cast or rapidly solidified equiatomic FeCoNi alloy while retaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or rapidly cooled equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected only when the annealing is precisely controlled to avoid coarsening or loss of high-entropy characteristics. Deviations in temperature or duration that lead to excessive grain growth or phase decomposition may nullify the desired increase in coercivity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the coercivity enhancement is uncertain due to potential variability in microstructural evolution kinetics during annealing. Optimization of the thermal treatment parameters is necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of as-cast or rapidly cooled equiatomic FeCoNi alloy (baseline) and another set subjected to the prescribed subsolvus annealing treatment. Characterize both sets by performing magnetic hysteresis measurements at room temperature and microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM or XRD) to assess the presence of nanoscale ordering or coherent precipitates.
measurements: Magnetometry to measure the coercive field using hysteresis loop characterization
Microstructural analysis (TEM/XRD) to verify the formation of nanoscale ordered domains or precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the annealed sample does not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity compared to the baseline, or if the expected nanoscale ordering/coherent precipitate formation is absent or accompanied by detrimental phase coarsening or loss of high-entropy characteristics.

frame.system: An fcc FeCoNi‐based high-entropy alloy that initially exhibits high saturation magnetization and low coercivity, similar to the baseline FeCoNi alloy, but modified to meet equiatomic and ≥1.0R configurational entropy criteria.
frame.goal: To obtain an alloy variant with considerably increased coercivity relative to both the original FeCoNi alloy and its Pd- and Pt-containing soft ferromagnetic derivatives.
frame.limitation: Previous interventions—namely, incorporating Pd or Pt to form FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt—yielded alloys that, although meeting compositional high-entropy criteria, maintained soft ferromagnetic behavior with a low coercive field.
root_cause_cues: FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt exhibited soft ferromagnetism
almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R
constraints: The final alloy must be an almost equiatomic multicomponent high-entropy alloy
It must maintain a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R
Any intervention must be a single change (i.e. not a multi-step alloying process) that is compatible with the baseline FeCoNi system
frame.regime: Operating within the fcc phase at room temperature (or standard magnetization test temperatures) under typical magnetic field cycling conditions. The intervention is intended to work in a thermally stable regime where controlled microstructural modifications (e.g. precipitation or ordering) can be induced without upsetting the overall high-entropy, equiatomic balance.
prior_attempts: The incorporation of heavier noble metals Pd and Pt in FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt was attempted to modify magnetic behavior, but resulted in alloys with soft magnetic responses (i.e. low coercivity), possibly due to reduced magnetocrystalline anisotropy or insufficient domain wall pinning.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis seeks to explain how a single, targeted microstructural intervention can enhance coercivity. It relies on established observations that increasing domain wall pinning—through mechanisms such as inducing nanoscale chemical ordering or coherent precipitation—can boost the magnetocrystalline anisotropy in ferromagnetic alloys.
frame.proposed_intervention: A single intervention hypothesis is to apply a controlled, subsolvus annealing treatment to the nearly equiatomic FeCoNi alloy, aimed at triggering nanoscale chemical ordering (or the in situ formation of coherent, finely dispersed precipitates) without altering the average equiatomic composition. This controlled annealing is predicted to introduce local lattice distortions and create nanoscale phase boundaries that act as domain wall pinning centers, thereby increasing the coercive field.
frame.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast or rapidly solidified baseline FeCoNi alloy, the annealed alloy should display a clear increase in coercivity while retaining high saturation magnetization. The intervention would thus yield a material with improved magnetic hardness suitable for permanent magnet applications, compared to the soft magnetic behavior seen in the Pd- and Pt-containing derivatives.
frame.experimental_conditions: The annealing treatment should be performed at a temperature selected to be below the threshold for phase coarsening yet high enough to allow atomic mobility for ordering (e.g., in the range of 500–700 °C) and for a duration sufficient to form the desired nanostructure. Magnetic characterization should be carried out at room temperature using standard hysteresis loop measurements.
frame.discriminating_experiment: Prepare two sets of samples: one set is the baseline equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy (with or without inert rapid cooling) and the other is the same alloy subjected to the prescribed subsolvus annealing treatment. Using magnetometry, measure and compare the coercive fields. The experiment is falsified if the annealed sample does not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity relative to the baseline sample, or if the induced nanostructuring adversely affects saturation magnetization or overall phase stability.

decision.trend: Initial attempts to modify the FeCoNi system focused on changing the composition by noble metal (Pd, Pt) additions to satisfy the high-entropy criteria but resulted in soft ferromagnetic behavior with low coercivity. In parallel, work on other high‐entropy alloys has shown that controlled thermal and thermomechanical treatments can induce nanoscale chemical ordering or coherent precipitation—with these microstructure features serving as domain‐wall pinning centers and enhancing mechanical strength. The ordered/precipitate structures achieved via subsolvus annealing (as detailed in PMC10213035) illustrate a successful strategy in tailoring the internal architecture of HEAs without altering their overall equiatomic character.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge in the FeCoNi-based system is how to enhance the coercive field—by introducing effective microstructural barriers to domain motion—without disrupting the nearly equiatomic composition and the required configurational entropy. The prior composition modifications (e.g. Pd, Pt additions) failed to create the necessary lattice distortions or phase boundaries required for domain wall pinning, leaving the mechanism of inducing coercivity through processing-induced nanoscale ordering experimentally unvalidated in the magnetic FeCoNi context.
decision.lever: subsolvus annealing treatment designed to trigger nanoscale chemical ordering or the in situ formation of coherent, finely-dispersed precipitates
decision.why: This lever follows the trend where single-step processing routes have been successfully used in other HEA systems to tailor nanoscale microstructures that act as pinning centers—thereby increasing coercivity. By selecting an annealing temperature (e.g., 500–700 °C) that is high enough to mobilize atoms yet below the coarsening threshold, the approach preserves equiatomic balance and high configurational entropy while introducing lattice distortions that impede domain wall motion, directly addressing the failure of previous Pd- and Pt-based composition changes.
